title: Chapter 77 — The Great Heidelburgh Tun
paragraphs: Now comes the baling of the case. But to understand it properly, you must know something of the curious internal structure of the thing being operated upon.

Regarding the Sperm Whale's head as a solid oblong, you may divide it sideways, along an inclined plane, into two quoins,* of which the lower is the bony structure forming the skull and jaws, and the upper an oily mass entirely free of bones, its broad forward end forming the expanded, vertical, apparent forehead of the whale. At the middle of the forehead, subdivide this upper quoin horizontally, and you then have two almost equal parts, which were already naturally divided by an internal wall of a thick, tendinous substance.

*Quoin is not a Euclidean term. It belongs to pure nautical mathematics. I am not aware that it has been defined before. A quoin is a solid which differs from a wedge in having its sharp end formed by the steep slant of one side, instead of by both sides tapering toward each other.

The lower subdivided part, called the junk, is one immense honeycomb of oil, formed throughout its whole extent by tough, elastic white fibers crossing and recrossing into ten thousand infiltrated cells. The upper part, known as the Case, may be regarded as the great Heidelburgh Tun of the Sperm Whale, after the famous giant wine-cask of that name. And as that famous great cask is mystically carved in front, so the whale's vast pleated forehead forms countless strange devices for the emblematic adornment of his wondrous tun. Moreover, as the Tun of Heidelburgh was always kept filled with the most excellent of the wines of the Rhine valleys, so the tun of the whale contains by far the most precious of all his oily vintages; namely, the highly prized spermaceti, in its absolutely pure, limpid and fragrant state. Nor is this precious substance found unmixed in any other part of the creature. Though in life it remains perfectly fluid, yet on exposure to the air after death it soon begins to solidify, sending out beautiful crystalline shoots, as when the first thin, delicate ice is just forming in water. A large whale's case generally yields about five hundred gallons of sperm, though, owing to unavoidable circumstances, a good deal of it is spilled, leaks and dribbles away, or is otherwise irretrievably lost in the ticklish business of securing what you can.

I don't know what fine and costly material lined the inside of the Heidelburgh Tun, but in sheer richness that lining could never have matched the silky, pearl-colored membrane, like the lining of an elegant fur-trimmed cloak, that forms the inner surface of the Sperm Whale's case.

It will have been seen that the Heidelburgh Tun of the Sperm Whale takes in the whole length of the entire top of the head; and since — as has been set out elsewhere — the head takes up one third of the whole length of the creature, then, putting that length at eighty feet for a good-sized whale, you have more than twenty-six feet for the depth of the tun when it is hoisted lengthwise, up and down, against a ship's side.

Since, in beheading the whale, the operator's instrument is brought close to the spot where an entrance is later forced into the spermaceti magazine, he has to be uncommonly careful, lest a careless, untimely stroke should invade the sanctuary and wastefully let out its invaluable contents. It is this beheaded end of the head, too, that is at last raised out of the water and held in that position by the enormous cutting tackles, whose hempen combinations, on one side, make quite a wilderness of ropes in that quarter.
Thus much being said, attend now, I ask you, to that marvelous and — in this particular instance — almost fatal operation whereby the Sperm Whale's great Heidelburgh Tun is tapped.
